chapters.title: 14. Glory to the Rooster!
paragraphs: His nerves gave out, as they say, and Rimsky did not wait for the report to be finished but fled to his office. He sat at his desk, staring with inflamed eyes at the magic ten-rouble notes lying in front of him. The financial director’s mind was reeling. Outside, a steady roar rolled on. The audience was pouring out of the Variety building into the street in streams. Suddenly the financial director’s extraordinarily sharpened hearing caught the distinct trill of a police whistle. In itself that sound never promises anything pleasant. And when it was repeated, and a second whistle, more commanding and more prolonged, came to its aid, and then a clearly audible guffawing joined in, and even some sort of hooting and whooping, the financial director understood at once that something else scandalous and nasty had happened in the street. And that this, however much one might like to wave it away, was most intimately connected with the disgusting performance given by the black magician and his assistants. The sensitive financial director was not in the least mistaken.
The moment he glanced out of the window that looked onto Sadovaya, his face twisted, and he did not whisper but hissed:
“I knew it!”

In the bright light of the powerful street lamps he saw on the pavement below him a lady wearing nothing but a slip and a pair of violet knickers. True, the lady had a little hat on her head and an umbrella in her hands.

Around this lady, who was in a state of utter confusion, now crouching down, now making as if to run off somewhere, a crowd surged, giving off that very laughter which sent a chill down the financial director’s spine. Next to the lady some citizen was rushing about, tearing off his summer coat and, in his agitation, quite unable to manage the sleeve, in which his arm had got stuck.

Shouts and roaring laughter came from another spot as well—namely from the left entrance—and, turning his head that way, Grigory Danilovich saw a second lady, in pink underwear. She leapt from the roadway onto the pavement, trying to hide in the doorway, but the audience streaming out blocked her way, and the poor victim of her own frivolity and passion for clothes, deceived by the firm of the vile Fagot, dreamed of only one thing—of sinking through the earth. A policeman was rushing toward the unfortunate woman, drilling the air with his whistle, and behind the policeman hurried some exceedingly merry young men in caps. It was they who were giving off that very laughter and hooting.
A thin, moustached cabby flew up to the first undressed lady and reined in his bony, broken-down horse with a flourish. The moustached man’s face was grinning with joy.
Rimsky struck himself on the head with his fist, spat, and sprang back from the window.

He sat at the desk for some time, listening to the street. The whistling at various points reached its height and then began to die down. The scandal, to Rimsky’s surprise, was somehow cleared up unexpectedly quickly.

The time had come to act; he would have to drink the bitter cup of responsibility. The telephones had been repaired during the third part of the show; he would have to call, report what had happened, ask for help, lie his way out, blame everything on Likhodeyev, shield himself, and so on. Pah, the devil!

Twice the upset director put his hand on the receiver, and twice he took it away again. And suddenly, in the dead silence of the office, the telephone itself burst out ringing right in the financial director’s face, and he started and went cold. “My nerves are in a fine state, though,” he thought, and picked up the receiver. At once he recoiled from it and turned whiter than paper. A quiet, at the same time insinuating and depraved woman’s voice whispered into the receiver:
“Don’t call anyone, Rimsky, or it will go badly...”

The line instantly went empty. Feeling goose bumps crawl down his back, the financial director put down the receiver and for some reason looked round at the window behind him. Through the sparse branches of the maple, still only faintly covered in green, he saw the moon racing through a transparent little cloud. For some reason his eyes fastened on the branches, and Rimsky looked at them, and the longer he looked, the more and more strongly fear took hold of him.

With an effort, the financial director at last turned away from the moonlit window and stood up. There could no longer be any question of telephoning, and now the financial director thought of only one thing—how to get out of the theatre as quickly as possible.

He listened: the theatre building was silent. Rimsky realized that he had long been alone on the whole second floor, and at this thought a childish, irresistible fear seized him. He could not think without a shudder that he would now have to walk alone along the empty corridors and go down the stairs. Feverishly he snatched the hypnotist’s ten-rouble notes from the desk, hid them in his briefcase, and coughed to cheer himself up even a tiny bit. The cough came out hoarse and weak.

And here it seemed to him that a rotten dampness was suddenly seeping in from under the office door. A shiver ran down the financial director’s spine. And then, on top of that, the clock unexpectedly struck and began to chime midnight. And even the chiming made the financial director shiver. But his heart sank completely when he heard a latchkey quietly turning in the lock of the door. Clutching his briefcase with damp, cold hands, the financial director felt that if this rustling in the keyhole lasted a little longer, he would not be able to bear it and would give a piercing scream.

At last the door yielded to someone’s efforts, opened, and Varenukha came noiselessly into the office. Rimsky sat down in the armchair just where he stood, because his legs gave way. Drawing a breath into his chest, he smiled a sort of ingratiating smile and said softly:
“God, how you frightened me...”
Yes, this sudden appearance could have frightened anyone, and yet at the same time it was a great joy: at least one loose end had stuck out in this tangled business.
“Well, speak, quickly! Well! Well!” Rimsky croaked, clutching at this loose end. “What does all this mean?!”
“Forgive me, please,” the newcomer responded in a hollow voice, closing the door, “I thought you’d already gone.”
And Varenukha, without taking off his cap, walked over to the armchair and sat down on the other side of the desk.

It must be said that Varenukha’s answer showed a slight oddity, which at once pricked the financial director, whose sensitivity could rival the seismograph of any of the best stations in the world. How could that be? Why would Varenukha come to the financial director’s office if he supposed he was not there? After all, he had his own office. That was one. And second: whichever entrance Varenukha had come into the building by, he would inevitably have met one of the night watchmen, and they had all been told that Grigory Danilovich would be staying on in his office for a while.
But the financial director did not ponder this oddity for long. He had no time for that.
“Why didn’t you call? What’s all this nonsense with Yalta about?”
“Well, just what I said,” replied the administrator, smacking his lips as though a bad tooth were bothering him. “They found him in a tavern in Pushkino.”
“What do you mean, in Pushkino?! That’s just outside Moscow? And the telegrams from Yalta?!”
“Yalta, the devil it was! He got the Pushkino telegraph clerk drunk, and the two of them started making mischief, including sending telegrams marked ‘Yalta.’”

“Aha... aha... Well, all right, all right...” Rimsky did not so much say as sing. His eyes lit up with a little yellow light. In his head a festive picture took shape: Styopa’s shameful dismissal from his post. Liberation! The financial director’s long-awaited liberation from this calamity in the person of Likhodeyev! And perhaps Stepan Bogdanovich would earn himself something even worse than dismissal... “Details!” said Rimsky, banging the paperweight on the desk.

And Varenukha began to give the details. As soon as he had arrived where the financial director had sent him, he was received at once and listened to with the utmost attention. Of course, nobody so much as entertained the thought that Styopa might be in Yalta. Everyone immediately agreed with Varenukha’s suggestion that Likhodeyev was, of course, at the “Yalta” in Pushkino.
“So where is he now?” the agitated financial director interrupted the administrator.
“Well, where else would he be?” answered the administrator with a crooked grin. “In the sobering-up station, naturally.”
“Well, well! Oh, thank you!”

And Varenukha went on with his tale. And the more he told, the more vividly there unrolled before the financial director a very long chain of Likhodeyev’s boorish acts and outrages, and every link in this chain was worse than the one before. What a thing it was, for a start, the drunken dance arm in arm with the telegraph clerk on the lawn in front of the Pushkino telegraph office, to the strains of some vagrant accordion! The chase after some citizenesses squealing with terror! The attempt to pick a fight with the barman in the “Yalta” itself! The scattering of green onions over the floor of that same “Yalta.” The smashing of eight bottles of dry white Ai-Danil. The breaking of the meter of a taxi driver who had refused to give Styopa his car. The threat to arrest the citizens who tried to put a stop to Styopa’s filthy antics... In a word, sheer black horror!

Styopa was well known in the theatrical circles of Moscow, and everyone knew that the man was no gift. But all the same, what the administrator was telling about him was too much even for Styopa. Yes, too much. Even very much too much...

Rimsky’s prickly eyes cut across the desk into the administrator’s face, and the further he went, the darker those eyes became. The more lifelike and colorful the vile details with which the administrator decked out his story, the less the financial director believed the storyteller. And when Varenukha reported that Styopa had run so wild that he had tried to resist those who had come to take him back to Moscow, the financial director already knew for certain that everything the administrator, returning at midnight, was telling him—everything—was a lie! A lie from the first word to the last.

Varenukha had not gone to Pushkino, and Styopa himself had not been in Pushkino either. There had been no drunken telegraph clerk, no broken glass in the tavern, Styopa had not been tied up with ropes...—none of it had happened.

The moment the financial director became firmly convinced that the administrator was lying to him, fear crept over his body, starting at his feet, and twice, once again, the financial director fancied that a rotten, malarial dampness was drifting along the floor. Never for an instant taking his eyes off the administrator, who was writhing somehow strangely in the armchair, all the time trying not to move out of the blue shadow of the desk lamp, and shielding himself in a remarkable way with a newspaper, supposedly from the light of the bulb, which was bothering him—the financial director thought of only one thing: what on earth did all this mean? Why was the administrator, who had come back to him far too late, lying to him so brazenly in the deserted and silent building? And an awareness of danger, an unknown but menacing danger, began to oppress the financial director’s soul. Pretending not to notice the administrator’s dodges and his tricks with the newspaper, the financial director studied his face, hardly listening any longer to what Varenukha was spinning. There was something that seemed even more inexplicable than the slanderous tale of adventures in Pushkino, invented for who knew what purpose, and that something was a change in the administrator’s appearance and manners.

However much he pulled the duck-bill peak of his cap down over his eyes to cast a shadow on his face, however much he twisted the newspaper sheet about, the financial director managed to make out an enormous bruise on the right side of his face, right by the nose. Besides that, the administrator, usually full-blooded, was now pale with a chalky, unhealthy pallor, and on this stifling night an old striped scarf had for some reason been wound around his neck. And if to this one added the disgusting habit of sucking and smacking his lips, which the administrator had acquired during his absence, the sharp change in his voice, which had become hollow and coarse, and the furtive cowardice in his eyes, one could safely say that Ivan Savelyevich Varenukha had become unrecognizable.

Something else was burningly troubling the financial director, but what exactly he could not make out, however much he strained his inflamed brain, however hard he peered at Varenukha. One thing he could affirm: there was something unheard-of, something unnatural, in this combination of the administrator and the all too familiar armchair.
“Well, we got the better of him at last, loaded him into the car,” droned Varenukha, peeping out from behind the sheet and covering the bruise with his palm.

Rimsky suddenly stretched out his hand and, as if absent-mindedly, drumming his fingers on the desk at the same time, pressed the button of the electric bell with his palm—and froze. In the empty building the sharp signal would certainly have been heard. But no signal followed, and the button sank lifelessly into the desktop. The button was dead, the bell broken.
The financial director’s ruse did not escape Varenukha, who asked, with a twitch, and an unmistakable spiteful fire flickering in his eyes:
“What are you ringing for?”
“Absent-mindedly,” the financial director replied hollowly, jerking his hand back, and in his turn asked in an unsteady voice: “What’s that on your face?”
“The car skidded, I hit myself on the door handle,” answered Varenukha, looking away.
“He’s lying!” the financial director exclaimed in his mind. And then suddenly his eyes grew round and utterly mad, and he stared at the back of the armchair.

Behind the armchair, on the floor, lay two crossed shadows, one denser and blacker, the other faint and gray. The shadow of the chair’s back and its tapered legs could be seen distinctly on the floor, but above the back there was no shadow of Varenukha’s head on the floor, just as under the legs there were no feet of the administrator.
“He casts no shadow!” Rimsky cried out desperately in his mind. A fit of trembling struck him.
Varenukha glanced furtively behind the back of the armchair, following Rimsky’s mad gaze, and understood that he had been found out.
He rose from the armchair (the financial director did the same) and stepped back a pace from the desk, clutching the briefcase in his hands.

“You’ve guessed, damn you! You were always a sharp one,” said Varenukha, grinning spitefully right into the financial director’s face, then unexpectedly sprang from the armchair to the door and quickly pushed down the button of the latch lock. The financial director looked round in despair, backing toward the window that gave onto the garden, and in that window, flooded with moonlight, he saw the face of a naked girl pressed to the glass, and her naked arm, thrust through the small upper pane, trying to open the lower catch. The upper one was already open.

It seemed to Rimsky that the light in the desk lamp was going out and that the desk was tilting. An icy wave broke over Rimsky, but, luckily for him, he mastered himself and did not fall. What remained of his strength was enough for him to whisper, but not to shout:
“Help...”

Varenukha, guarding the door, was hopping up and down beside it, hanging in the air for long moments and swaying there. With crooked fingers he waved toward Rimsky, hissed and smacked his lips, and winked at the girl in the window.

She began to hurry, thrust her red head through the small pane, stretched out her arm as far as she could, began scratching at the lower bolt with her nails and shaking the frame. Her arm started to lengthen, like rubber, and became covered with a corpse-like green. At last the dead woman’s green fingers grasped the head of the bolt, turned it, and the frame began to open. Rimsky gave a weak cry, leaned against the wall, and held out his briefcase in front of him like a shield. He understood that his end had come.

The frame swung wide open, but instead of the freshness of the night and the scent of the lindens, the smell of a cellar burst into the room. The dead woman stepped onto the windowsill. Rimsky clearly saw the spots of decay on her breast.

And at that moment the joyful, unexpected crowing of a rooster came flying from the garden, from that low building behind the shooting gallery where the birds that took part in the shows were kept. The loud-throated trained rooster was trumpeting the news that dawn was rolling toward Moscow from the east.
Wild fury distorted the girl’s face; she let out a hoarse curse, and Varenukha by the door gave a shriek and crashed down out of the air onto the floor.

The rooster crowed again, the girl clacked her teeth, and her red hair stood on end. At the third crow of the rooster she turned and flew out. And after her, springing up and stretching out horizontally in the air, looking like a flying cupid, Varenukha floated slowly out of the window over the desk.

White as snow, without a single dark hair, the old man who only a short while ago had been Rimsky ran to the door, undid the button, opened the door and rushed off along the dark corridor. At the turn to the staircase, moaning with fear, he groped for the switch, and the staircase lit up. On the stairs the shaking, trembling old man fell, because it seemed to him that Varenukha had softly come crashing down on him from above.

Running downstairs, Rimsky saw the watchman, who had fallen asleep on a chair by the box office in the lobby. Rimsky crept past him on tiptoe and slipped out through the main door. In the street he felt somewhat better. He came to his senses so far that, clutching his head, he managed to realize that his hat had been left in the office.

It goes without saying that he did not go back for it but, gasping for breath, ran across the wide street to the opposite corner by the cinema, near which a dim reddish light was hovering. A minute later he was already beside it. Nobody had managed to grab the car first.
“To the Leningrad express, I’ll tip you,” the old man said, breathing heavily and holding his heart.
“I’m going to the garage,” the driver answered with hatred and turned away.
Then Rimsky unbuckled his briefcase, pulled out fifty roubles and held them out to the driver through the open front window.

A few moments later the rattling car was flying like a whirlwind along the Garden Ring. The passenger was tossed about on the seat, and in the shard of mirror hung in front of the driver Rimsky saw now the driver’s joyful eyes, now his own mad ones.
Leaping out of the car in front of the station building, Rimsky shouted to the first man he came across in a white apron, with a badge:
“First class, one, I’ll give you thirty,” crumpling them, he was pulling ten-rouble notes out of his briefcase, “if there’s no first, then second, if there’s none of that, take a hard seat.”
The man with the badge, glancing round at the illuminated clock, was tearing the ten-rouble notes out of Rimsky’s hands.
Five minutes later the express vanished from under the glass dome of the station and disappeared completely into the darkness. And Rimsky disappeared along with it.

chapters.title: 15. Nikanor Ivanovich’s Dream
paragraphs: It is not hard to guess that the fat man with the crimson face who had been put in room No. 119 at the clinic was Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy.
He did not, however, come to Professor Stravinsky straight away, but only after first spending some time in another place.
Of this other place Nikanor Ivanovich retained little in his memory. All he remembered was a desk, a cupboard and a sofa.

There, with Nikanor Ivanovich, whose eyes kept clouding over from rushes of blood and agitation of spirit, a conversation was begun, but the conversation came out somehow strange and muddled, or, to put it better, did not come out at all.
The very first question put to Nikanor Ivanovich was this:
“You are Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy, chairman of the house committee at No. 302-bis on Sadovaya?”
To this Nikanor Ivanovich, laughing a terrible laugh, replied literally as follows:
“I’m Nikanor, of course I’m Nikanor! But what the deuce kind of chairman am I!”
“Meaning what?” they asked Nikanor Ivanovich, narrowing their eyes.

“Meaning this,” he answered, “that if I was a chairman, I ought to have established at once that he was the unclean power! Otherwise what is all this? Cracked pince-nez... all in rags... What kind of interpreter for a foreigner can he be!”
“Who are you talking about?” they asked Nikanor Ivanovich.
“Koroviev!” cried Nikanor Ivanovich. “He’s dug himself in at our apartment No. 50! Write it down: Koroviev. He must be caught immediately! Write it down: entrance six, that’s where he is.”
“Where did you get the foreign currency?” they asked Nikanor Ivanovich sincerely.

“The true God, God almighty,” Nikanor Ivanovich began, “sees everything, and it serves me right. I never held it in my hands and never suspected what sort of thing currency was! The Lord is punishing me for my foulness,” Nikanor Ivanovich went on with feeling, now buttoning his shirt, now unbuttoning it, now crossing himself. “I took! I took, but I took ours, Soviet money! I registered people for money, I won’t argue, it happened. And our secretary Prolezhnev is a fine one too, a fine one! Let’s say it straight: they’re all thieves in the house management. But currency I never took!”

At a request to stop playing the fool and tell how the dollars had got into the ventilation shaft, Nikanor Ivanovich went down on his knees and swayed, opening his mouth as if he wished to swallow a block of the parquet.
“If you like,” he bellowed, “I’ll eat dirt to prove I didn’t take it! And Koroviev—he’s the devil!”
There is a limit to all patience, and at the desk they had already raised their voices and hinted to Nikanor Ivanovich that it was time he started speaking in human language.
At this the room with that very sofa rang with a wild roar from Nikanor Ivanovich, who had jumped up from his knees:
“There he is! There he is behind the cupboard! There, he’s grinning! And his pince-nez... Hold him! Sprinkle the premises with holy water!”
The blood drained from Nikanor Ivanovich’s face; trembling, he made the sign of the cross in the air, dashed to the door and back, struck up some prayer, and at last started talking utter gibberish.
It became perfectly clear that Nikanor Ivanovich was fit for no conversation of any kind. He was led out and put in a separate room, where he calmed down somewhat and only prayed and sobbed.

They did, of course, go to Sadovaya and visit apartment No. 50. But they found no Koroviev there, and nobody in the building knew or had ever seen any Koroviev. The apartment occupied by the late Berlioz and by Likhodeyev, who had gone off to Yalta, was empty, and in the study the wax seals hung peacefully on the cupboards, undamaged by anyone. And with that they left Sadovaya, and along with those who left went the bewildered and crushed secretary of the house management, Prolezhnev.

In the evening Nikanor Ivanovich was delivered to Stravinsky’s clinic. There he behaved so restlessly that he had to be given an injection according to Stravinsky’s prescription, and only after midnight did Nikanor Ivanovich fall asleep in room 119, now and then letting out a heavy, suffering moan.
But the further it went, the lighter his sleep became. He stopped tossing and groaning, began to breathe easily and evenly, and they left him alone.

Then Nikanor Ivanovich was visited by a dream, at the root of which, undoubtedly, lay his experiences of that day. It began with Nikanor Ivanovich seeing, as it were, some people with golden trumpets in their hands leading him, and very solemnly, up to a large lacquered door. At this door his companions seemed to play a fanfare in Nikanor Ivanovich’s honor, and then a booming bass voice from the heavens said merrily:
“Welcome, Nikanor Ivanovich! Hand over your currency!”
Extremely surprised, Nikanor Ivanovich saw a black loudspeaker above him.

Then for some reason he found himself in a theatre auditorium, where crystal chandeliers shone beneath a gilded ceiling, and sconces on the walls. Everything was as it ought to be, as in a theatre small in size but very rich. There was a stage, closed off by a velvet curtain whose dark cherry ground was strewn, like little stars, with pictures of enlarged gold ten-rouble pieces; there was a prompter’s box, and there was even an audience.

What surprised Nikanor Ivanovich was that this whole audience was of one sex—the male—and all of them, for some reason, had beards. Besides that, it was striking that there were no chairs in the auditorium, and this whole audience was sitting on the floor, which was splendidly polished and slippery.

Embarrassed in this new and large company, Nikanor Ivanovich, after shifting about for a while, followed the general example and sat down cross-legged on the parquet, settling himself between some hefty red-bearded fellow and another, pale and very overgrown citizen. None of those sitting there paid any attention to the newly arrived spectator.

Then the soft ring of a little bell was heard, the lights in the auditorium went out, the curtain parted, and a lit stage was revealed, with an armchair, a little table on which stood a golden bell, and a solid black velvet backdrop.

At this an artiste in a dinner jacket came out from the wings, clean-shaven and with his hair parted, young and with very pleasant features. The audience in the hall livened up and everyone turned toward the stage. The artiste walked up to the prompter’s box and rubbed his hands.
“Still sitting?” he asked in a soft baritone, and smiled at the house.
“We’re sitting, we’re sitting,” the tenors and basses answered him in chorus from the hall.

“Hm...” the artiste began pensively, “and how is it you don’t get bored, I don’t understand? Everybody else, like normal people, is out walking in the streets just now, enjoying the spring sunshine and warmth, and here you are stuck on the floor in a stuffy hall! Is the program really so interesting? However, to each his own,” the artiste concluded philosophically.
Then he changed both the timbre of his voice and his intonation, and announced gaily and resonantly:
“And so, the next number on our program: Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy, chairman of a house committee and manager of a dietary canteen. A warm welcome, please, for Nikanor Ivanovich!”

Unanimous applause was the answer to the artiste. Astonished, Nikanor Ivanovich goggled, while the master of ceremonies, shielding his eyes with his hand from the glare of the footlights, found him with his gaze among those sitting there and beckoned him tenderly onto the stage with a finger. And Nikanor Ivanovich, without knowing how, found himself on the stage. The light of colored lamps struck his eyes from below and in front, so that the hall with its audience at once sank into darkness.
“Well, now, Nikanor Ivanovich, set us an example,” the young artiste said sincerely, “and hand over your currency.”
Silence fell. Nikanor Ivanovich caught his breath and began quietly:
“I swear to God that...”
But before he had got these words out, the whole hall burst into shouts of indignation. Nikanor Ivanovich lost his head and fell silent.
“As far as I understood you,” said the host of the program, “you were about to swear to God that you have no currency?” And he looked sympathetically at Nikanor Ivanovich.
“Exactly so, I haven’t,” replied Nikanor Ivanovich.

“I see,” responded the artiste, “but forgive my indiscretion: then where did the four hundred dollars come from that were found in the lavatory of the apartment whose only occupants are you and your spouse?”
“Magic dollars!” someone in the dark hall said, with obvious irony.

“Exactly so, magic,” Nikanor Ivanovich answered timidly, addressing no one in particular, whether the artiste or the dark hall, and explained: “The unclean power, the checked interpreter planted them on me.”
And again the hall roared with indignation. When silence fell, the artiste said:
“Just listen to the La Fontaine fables I have to put up with! Four hundred dollars planted on him! Now you here are all currency dealers, and I address you as experts: is such a thing conceivable?”
“We’re not currency dealers,” a few offended voices rang out in the theatre, “but the thing is inconceivable.”
“I agree entirely,” said the artiste firmly, “and I will ask you: what can be planted on somebody, or left on a doorstep?”
“A baby!” someone shouted from the hall.

“Absolutely right,” the host of the program confirmed, “a baby, an anonymous letter, a leaflet, an infernal machine, who knows what else, but nobody is going to plant four hundred dollars on anyone, for no such idiot exists in nature.” And, turning to Nikanor Ivanovich, the artiste added reproachfully and sadly: “You’ve upset me, Nikanor Ivanovich! And I was counting on you. And so our number has not come off.”
Whistles aimed at Nikanor Ivanovich rang out in the hall.
“He’s a currency dealer!” they shouted in the hall. “It’s because of people like him that innocent folk like us have to suffer!”
“Don’t scold him,” the master of ceremonies said gently, “he will repent.” And, turning his blue eyes, full of tears, on Nikanor Ivanovich, he added: “Well, go back to your place, Nikanor Ivanovich.”
After this the artiste rang the bell and announced loudly:
“Intermission, you scoundrels!”

Shaken, Nikanor Ivanovich, who to his own surprise had become a participant in some theatrical program, found himself back in his place on the floor. Then he dreamed that the hall was plunged into total darkness and that red burning words leapt out on the walls: “Hand over your currency!” Then the curtain opened again and the master of ceremonies invited:
“Sergei Gerardovich Dunchil to the stage, please.”
Dunchil turned out to be a respectable-looking but badly neglected man of about fifty.

“Sergei Gerardovich,” the master of ceremonies addressed him, “for a month and a half now you have been sitting here, stubbornly refusing to hand over the currency you still have, while the country is in need of it and you have no use for it whatsoever, and still you persist. You are an educated man, you understand all this perfectly well, and yet you won’t meet me halfway.”
“Unfortunately, I can do nothing, since I have no more currency,” Dunchil answered calmly.
“Then haven’t you, at least, some diamonds?” asked the artiste.
“No diamonds either.”

The artiste hung his head and fell to thinking, and then clapped his hands. From the wings a middle-aged lady came out onto the stage, dressed in the fashion, that is, in a coat without a collar and a tiny hat. The lady looked alarmed, while Dunchil glanced at her without moving an eyebrow.
“Who is this lady?” the host of the program asked Dunchil.
“This is my wife,” Dunchil replied with dignity, and looked at the lady’s long neck with a certain distaste.
“We have troubled you, Madame Dunchil,” the master of ceremonies turned to the lady, “for the following reason: we wished to ask you whether your spouse has any more currency?”
“He handed it all over that time,” Madame Dunchil answered nervously.

“I see,” said the artiste, “well, then, if that is so, so be it. If he has handed it all over, then we must part with Sergei Gerardovich immediately; what can one do! If you please, you may leave the theatre, Sergei Gerardovich,” and the artiste made a regal gesture.
Calmly and with dignity, Dunchil turned and walked toward the wings.
“One little minute!” the master of ceremonies stopped him. “Allow me, by way of farewell, to show you one more number from our program,” and again he clapped his hands.

The black rear curtain parted, and onto the stage came a young beauty in a ball gown, holding a little golden tray on which lay a thick bundle tied with candy-box ribbon and a diamond necklace from which blue, yellow and red fires leapt in all directions.
Dunchil took a step back and his face went pale. The hall froze.

“Eighteen thousand dollars and a necklace worth forty thousand in gold,” the artiste announced solemnly, “were kept by Sergei Gerardovich in the city of Kharkov, in the apartment of his mistress, Ida Herculanovna Vors, whom we have the pleasure of seeing before us, and who kindly helped to discover these treasures, priceless, yet pointless in the hands of a private person. Thank you very much, Ida Herculanovna.”
The beauty smiled, flashing her teeth, and her shaggy eyelashes fluttered.

“And beneath your mask of dignity,” the artiste turned to Dunchil, “there hides a greedy spider and an astounding swindler and liar. In a month and a half you have worn everyone out with your obtuse stubbornness. Go home now, and may the hell your spouse will arrange for you be your punishment.”
Dunchil swayed and seemed about to collapse, but someone’s sympathetic hands caught him. At this the front curtain came crashing down and hid all those on the stage.

Frenzied applause shook the hall so that it seemed to Nikanor Ivanovich that the lights were jumping in the chandeliers. And when the front curtain went up, there was no longer anyone on the stage except the lone artiste. He drew a second volley of applause, bowed, and began to speak:

“In the person of this Dunchil, you have seen a typical ass perform in our program. After all, I had the pleasure of saying yesterday that the secret hoarding of currency is nonsense. Nobody can make use of it under any circumstances, I assure you. Take this Dunchil, for instance. He receives a splendid salary and wants for nothing. He has a fine apartment, a wife and a beautiful mistress. But no! Instead of living quietly and peacefully, without any unpleasantness, by handing over the currency and the stones, this mercenary blockhead got himself exposed in front of everyone after all, and for dessert acquired the biggest of family troubles. And so, who will hand over? Nobody willing? In that case, the next number on our program: that celebrated dramatic talent, the artiste Savva Potapovich Kurolesov, especially invited, will perform excerpts from The Covetous Knight by the poet Pushkin.”
The promised Kurolesov was not slow to appear on the stage and turned out to be a tall, fleshy, clean-shaven man in tails and a white tie.
Without any preamble he put on a gloomy face, knitted his brows and began to speak in an unnatural voice, glancing sidelong at the golden bell:
“As a young rake awaits his assignation with some sly harlot of depraved desire...”

And Kurolesov told a great many bad things about himself. Nikanor Ivanovich heard Kurolesov confess that some unhappy widow, howling, had knelt before him in the rain but had not touched the artiste’s callous heart.

Before his dream Nikanor Ivanovich had known absolutely nothing of the works of the poet Pushkin, but he knew the man himself perfectly well, and several times a day he would utter phrases like: “And is Pushkin going to pay the rent, then?” or “So it was Pushkin who unscrewed the light bulb on the stairs, was it?” or “So Pushkin’s going to buy the fuel oil, is he?”

Now, having become acquainted with one of his works, Nikanor Ivanovich grew sad, pictured to himself the woman on her knees, with orphans, in the rain, and could not help thinking: “What a character that Kurolesov is, though!”

And he, raising his voice all the while, went on repenting and thoroughly confused Nikanor Ivanovich, because he suddenly began addressing someone who was not on the stage, and answered himself on behalf of this absent person, calling himself now “sovereign,” now “baron,” now “father,” now “son,” now with the formal “you,” now with the familiar one.
Nikanor Ivanovich understood only one thing: that the artiste died an evil death, crying out, “The keys! My keys!” and collapsing on the floor after this, wheezing and carefully tearing off his tie.
Having died, Kurolesov got up, brushed the dust off his tailcoat trousers, bowed, smiling a false smile, and withdrew to thin applause. And the master of ceremonies said this:

“We have just heard The Covetous Knight in the remarkable performance of Savva Potapovich. This knight hoped that sportive nymphs would come running to him, and that a great many more pleasant things in the same vein would happen. But, as you see, none of this occurred: no nymphs came running to him, and the muses brought him no tribute, and he raised no palaces of any kind, but, on the contrary, ended very badly—he dropped dead—to the devil with him—of a stroke on his chest full of currency and stones. I warn you that something of the kind will happen to you too, if not worse, if you don’t hand over your currency!”
Whether it was Pushkin’s poetry that made such an impression or the prosaic speech of the master of ceremonies, but suddenly a shy voice rang out from the hall:
“I’ll hand over my currency.”
“Be so kind as to come up on the stage,” the master of ceremonies invited politely, peering into the dark hall.
And on the stage appeared a short, fair-haired citizen who, judging by his face, had not shaved for about three weeks.
“Excuse me, what is your name?” the master of ceremonies inquired.
“Kanavkin, Nikolai,” the newcomer responded shyly.
“Ah! A pleasure, citizen Kanavkin. Well?”
“I’ll hand it over,” Kanavkin said quietly.
“How much?”
“A thousand dollars and twenty gold ten-rouble pieces.”
“Bravo! Is that all you have?”

The host of the program stared straight into Kanavkin’s eyes, and it even seemed to Nikanor Ivanovich that rays spurted from those eyes and pierced Kanavkin right through, like X-rays. The hall stopped breathing.

“I believe you!” the artiste exclaimed at last, and extinguished his gaze. “I believe you! These eyes do not lie. How many times have I told you that your basic mistake is that you underestimate the significance of human eyes. Understand that the tongue can conceal the truth, but the eyes—never! You are asked a sudden question, you don’t even flinch, in one second you take control of yourself and know what must be said to hide the truth, and you say it very convincingly, and not a single fold of your face stirs, but, alas, the truth, alarmed by the question, leaps for an instant from the bottom of your soul into your eyes, and it’s all over. It has been noticed, and you are caught!”
Having delivered, and with great fervor, this very convincing speech, the artiste tenderly inquired of Kanavkin:
“And where are they hidden?”
“At my aunt’s, Porokhovnikova’s, on Prechistenka...”
“Ah! That’s... wait... that’s Klavdia Ilyinichna’s, isn’t it?”
“Yes.”
“Ah, yes, yes, yes, yes! The little private house? With the little front garden opposite? Of course, I know it, I know it! And where did you stick them there?”
“In the cellar, in an Einem chocolate box...”
The artiste threw up his hands.

“Have you ever seen anything like it?” he cried in distress. “Why, they’ll go moldy there, they’ll get damp! Well, is it conceivable to entrust currency to such people? Eh? Just like children, honest to God!”
Kanavkin himself understood that he had blundered and put his foot in it, and hung his tufted head.

“Money,” the artiste went on, “ought to be kept in the State Bank, in special dry and well-guarded premises, and certainly not in an aunt’s cellar, where, in particular, the rats may damage it! Really, you ought to be ashamed, Kanavkin! You’re a grown man, after all.”
Kanavkin no longer knew where to put himself and only picked at the lapel of his jacket with his finger.

“Well, all right,” the artiste relented, “let bygones be bygones...” And suddenly he added unexpectedly: “Oh, by the way... so as to do it all in one go... so as not to send the car out for nothing... this same aunt has some too, hasn’t she, eh?”
Kanavkin, who had in no way expected such a turn of events, flinched, and silence fell in the theatre.

“Eh, Kanavkin,” the master of ceremonies said with tender reproach, “and here I was praising him! And there you go, he’s gone and stumbled out of the blue! It’s absurd, Kanavkin! I was only just talking about the eyes. Anyone can see the aunt has some. Well, why do you torment us for nothing?”
“She has!” Kanavkin cried recklessly.
“Bravo!” cried the master of ceremonies.
“Bravo!” the hall roared terribly.

When things had quieted down, the master of ceremonies congratulated Kanavkin, shook his hand, offered to have him driven home to town in a car, and ordered someone in the wings to call by for the aunt in that same car and ask her to kindly attend a program at the women’s theatre.

“Oh yes, I wanted to ask: didn’t your aunt say where she hides her own?” the master of ceremonies inquired, courteously offering Kanavkin a cigarette and a lighted match. Lighting up, the latter gave a rather dreary smirk.

“I believe you, I believe you,” the artiste responded with a sigh. “That old skinflint wouldn’t tell it to the devil, let alone her nephew. Well, then, we shall try to awaken human feelings in her. Perhaps not all the strings have rotted yet in her little usurer’s soul. All the best, Kanavkin!”
And the happy Kanavkin drove off. The artiste inquired whether there was anyone else who wished to hand over currency, but received silence in reply.
“Odd fellows, honest to God!” said the artiste with a shrug, and the curtain hid him.
The lamps went out, for a while there was darkness, and from far off in it could be heard a nervous tenor singing:
“There heaps of gold lie shining bright, and all of them are mine by right!”
Then, from somewhere, applause came faintly twice.

“Some little lady is handing hers over in the women’s theatre,” Nikanor Ivanovich’s red-bearded neighbor suddenly spoke up, and with a sigh he added: “Eh, if it weren’t for my geese!.. I’ve got fighting geese, my dear man, in Lianozovo... They’ll die without me, I’m afraid. A fighting bird, delicate, needs looking after... Eh, if it weren’t for the geese! You won’t surprise me with Pushkin,” and he started sighing again.

Here the hall lit up brightly, and Nikanor Ivanovich began dreaming that cooks in white hats and with ladles in their hands came pouring into the hall from all the doors. Kitchen boys dragged into the hall a vat of soup and a tray of sliced black bread. The spectators livened up. The merry cooks darted among the theatregoers, ladled soup into bowls and handed out bread.

“Eat your dinner, lads,” the cooks shouted, “and hand over your currency! Why sit here for nothing? Who’d want to slurp this swill! Go home, have a proper drink, a bite to go with it—that’s the life!”

“Now why, for instance, have you dug yourself in here, old fellow?” a fat cook with a raspberry-colored neck addressed Nikanor Ivanovich directly, holding out to him a bowl in which a single cabbage leaf floated in liquid.
“I haven’t got any! I haven’t! I haven’t got any!” Nikanor Ivanovich shouted in a terrible voice. “Understand, I haven’t!”
“You haven’t?” the cook roared in a menacing bass. “You haven’t?” he asked in a tender woman’s voice. “You haven’t, you haven’t,” he muttered soothingly, turning into the nurse Praskovya Fyodorovna.

She was gently shaking Nikanor Ivanovich by the shoulder as he moaned in his sleep. Then the cooks melted away, and the theatre with its curtain fell to pieces. Through his tears Nikanor Ivanovich made out his room in the hospital and two people in white coats, though by no means the cheeky cooks who poke their noses into people’s business with their advice, but the doctor and that same Praskovya Fyodorovna, holding in her hands not a bowl but a little dish covered with gauze, with a syringe lying on it.
“What is all this?” Nikanor Ivanovich said bitterly while they gave him the injection. “I haven’t got any, and that’s that! Let Pushkin hand over currency to them. I haven’t got any!”
“No, you haven’t, you haven’t,” the kind-hearted Praskovya Fyodorovna soothed him, “and where there’s none, there’s no case to answer.”
Nikanor Ivanovich felt better after the injection, and he fell asleep without any dreams at all.

But thanks to his shouts the alarm spread to room 120, where the patient woke up and began looking for his head, and to room 118, where the unknown master grew restless and wrung his hands in anguish, looking at the moon, remembering the bitter last autumn night of his life, the strip of light under the door in the basement, and the hair come loose from its curls.
From room 118 the alarm flew along the balcony to Ivan, and he woke up and wept.

But the doctor quickly calmed all the alarmed, those afflicted in the head, and they began to fall asleep. Ivan was the last of all to drift off, when it was already growing light over the river. After the medicine, which soaked into his whole body, calm came to him like a wave that covered him. His body grew lighter, and drowsiness fanned his head with a warm breeze. He fell asleep, and the last thing he heard while awake was the predawn twittering of birds in the forest. But they soon fell silent, and he began dreaming that the sun was already descending over Bald Mountain, and this mountain was cordoned off by a double cordon...

chapters.title: 16. The Execution
paragraphs: The sun was already descending over Bald Mountain, and this mountain was cordoned off by a double cordon.

The cavalry ala that had cut across the procurator’s path around noon came out at a trot to the Hebron Gate of the city. The way had already been prepared for it. The infantrymen of the Cappadocian cohort had pressed back to the sides the crowds of people, mules and camels, and the ala, trotting and raising white columns of dust to the sky, came out at the crossroads where two roads met: the southern one, leading to Bethlehem, and the northwestern one, to Jaffa. The ala raced along the northwestern road. The same Cappadocians were scattered along the edges of the road, and they had driven off it in good time all the caravans hurrying to the feast in Yershalaim. Crowds of pilgrims stood behind the Cappadocians, having left their temporary striped tents pitched right on the grass. After going about a kilometer, the ala overtook the second cohort of the Lightning Legion and, covering another kilometer, was the first to reach the foot of Bald Mountain. Here it dismounted. The commander split the ala into troops, and they cordoned off the whole foot of the low hill, leaving free only one way up it, from the Jaffa road.
After a while the second cohort came to the hill behind the ala, climbed one tier higher, and girdled the mountain like a crown.

At last the century under the command of Mark Ratslayer arrived. It came stretched out in two lines along the edges of the road, and between these lines, under escort of the secret guard, rode in a cart the three condemned men, with white boards around their necks, on each of which was written “Robber and rebel” in two languages, Aramaic and Greek.

Behind the cart of the condemned moved others, loaded with freshly hewn posts with crossbeams, ropes, shovels, buckets and axes. On these carts rode six executioners. Behind them on horseback rode the centurion Mark, the head of the Yershalaim temple guard, and that same man in the hood with whom Pilate had held a brief conference in the darkened room in the palace.

The procession was closed by a line of soldiers, and behind it walked some two thousand curious people who had not been frightened off by the hellish heat and wished to be present at the interesting spectacle.

These curious people from the city had now been joined by curious pilgrims, who were let through without hindrance to the tail of the procession. To the thin cries of the heralds who accompanied the column and called out what Pilate had called out around noon, it drew itself up onto Bald Mountain.

The ala let everyone through to the second tier, but the second century let through to the top only those who had to do with the execution, and then, maneuvering quickly, it dispersed the crowd around the whole hill, so that it found itself between the infantry cordon above and the cavalry one below. Now it could watch the execution through the loose line of infantrymen.

And so, more than three hours had passed since the procession had climbed the mountain, and the sun was already descending over Bald Mountain, but the heat was still unbearable, and the soldiers in both cordons suffered from it, languished with boredom, and in their hearts cursed the three robbers, sincerely wishing them the swiftest death.

The little commander of the ala, his forehead soaked and his white shirt dark with sweat on the back, who was stationed at the bottom of the hill by the open way up, kept going over to the leather bucket of the first troop, scooping water out of it in handfuls, drinking, and wetting his turban. Having got some relief from this, he would walk away and again begin pacing back and forth along the dusty road leading to the top. His long sword knocked against his laced leather boot. The commander wished to show his cavalrymen an example of endurance, but, taking pity on the soldiers, he allowed them to make pyramids of the lances stuck into the ground and throw their white cloaks over them. Under these shelters the Syrians hid from the merciless sun. The buckets emptied quickly, and cavalrymen from the different troops took turns going for water to the gully below the mountain, where, in the thin shade of scrawny mulberry trees, a muddy stream was living out its last days in this devilish heat. There too, catching the unsteady shade, stood the bored grooms, holding the horses, which had grown quiet.

The soldiers’ weariness and their curses against the robbers were understandable. The procurator’s fears about disorders that might occur during the execution in the city of Yershalaim, which he hated, had, fortunately, not been borne out. And when the fourth hour of the execution began to run, there remained between the two lines, the infantry above and the cavalry at the foot, contrary to all expectations, not a single person. The sun had burned up the crowd and driven it back to Yershalaim. Beyond the line of the two Roman centuries there were only two dogs, belonging to no one knew whom and come onto the hill for no one knew what reason. But the heat had overcome them too, and they lay down with their tongues hanging out, breathing heavily and paying no attention at all to the green-backed lizards, the only creatures not afraid of the sun, darting between the scorching stones and some sort of plants with large thorns that crept along the ground.

No one had made an attempt to rescue the condemned men, either in Yershalaim itself, flooded with troops, or here on the cordoned hill, and the crowd had gone back to the city, because there was indeed absolutely nothing interesting in this execution, while there in the city preparations were already under way for the great feast of Passover, which would begin that evening.

The Roman infantry on the second tier suffered even more than the cavalrymen. The only thing the centurion Ratslayer allowed the soldiers was to take off their helmets and cover their heads with white bands soaked in water, but he kept the soldiers standing, spears in hand. He himself, in the same kind of band, though not soaked but dry, strolled about not far from the group of executioners, not having removed even the silver lion masks sewn onto his shirt, nor his greaves, sword and knife. The sun beat straight down on the centurion without doing him any harm, and it was impossible to look at the lion masks: the eyes were eaten away by the blinding glitter of silver that seemed to be boiling in the sun.

Ratslayer’s mutilated face showed neither fatigue nor displeasure, and it seemed that the giant centurion was capable of walking like this all day, all night and another day—in short, as long as might be needed. Of walking just the same, his hands on his heavy belt with its copper plaques, just as sternly glancing now at the posts with the men being executed, now at the soldiers in the line, just as indifferently kicking aside with the toe of his shaggy boot the human bones bleached by time or the small flints that came under his feet.
That man in the hood had settled himself not far from the posts on a three-legged stool and sat in good-humored immobility, though now and then, out of boredom, he poked at the sand with a twig.

What was said about there being not a single person beyond the line of legionaries is not quite true. There was one person, it is just that not everyone could see him. He had settled himself not on the side where the way up the mountain was open, from which it was most convenient to watch the execution, but on the northern side, where the hill was not gently sloping and easy of access but uneven, where there were both hollows and crevices, there, where, clinging in a cleft to the waterless earth cursed by heaven, a sickly little fig tree was trying to live.

It was precisely under it, though it gave no shade whatsoever, that this sole spectator, and not participant, of the execution had established himself, and he had been sitting on a stone from the very beginning, that is, for nearly four hours now. Yes, to watch the execution he had chosen not the best but the worst position. Yet even from there the posts could be seen, and beyond the line the two glittering spots on the centurion’s chest could be seen too, and for a man who clearly wished to remain little noticed and disturbed by no one, this was evidently quite enough.

But about four hours earlier, at the beginning of the execution, this man had behaved quite differently and could very well have been noticed, which was probably why he had now changed his behavior and withdrawn on his own.

Back then, the moment the procession had passed through the line to the very top, he appeared for the first time, and moreover as a man who was clearly late. He was breathing heavily and was not walking but running up the hill, pushing his way along, and when he saw that the line had closed before him, as before everyone else, he made a naive attempt, pretending not to understand the irritated shouts, to break through between the soldiers to the very place of execution, where the condemned were already being taken down from the cart. For this he received a heavy blow in the chest from the blunt end of a spear and sprang back from the soldiers with a cry, not of pain but of despair. He gave the legionary who had struck him a dull look, utterly indifferent to everything, like a man insensible to physical pain.

Coughing and gasping for breath, holding his chest, he ran around the hill, trying to find on the northern side some gap in the line through which he could slip. But it was already too late. The ring had closed. And the man, his face distorted with grief, was forced to give up his attempts to break through to the carts, from which the posts had already been unloaded. These attempts would have led to nothing except his being seized, and to be detained on this day was in no way part of his plans.
And so he had gone off to the side, to the cleft, where it was quieter and no one bothered him.

Now, sitting on the stone, this black-bearded man, his eyes festering from the sun and from lack of sleep, was in anguish. Now he sighed, opening his tallith, worn out in his wanderings, which had turned from blue to a dirty gray, and bared his chest, bruised by the spear, down which dirty sweat was running; now, in unbearable torment, he raised his eyes to the sky, following the three vultures that had long been floating high above in great circles in anticipation of an imminent feast; now he fixed a hopeless gaze on the yellow earth and saw on it a half-crumbled dog’s skull and lizards running around it.
The man’s torments were so great that at times he began talking to himself.
“Oh, I am a fool!” he muttered, rocking on the stone in anguish of soul and scratching his swarthy chest with his nails. “A fool, a senseless woman, a coward! Carrion is what I am, not a man!”

He would fall silent, hang his head, then, having drunk some warm water from a wooden flask, revive again and clutch now at the knife hidden under the tallith on his chest, now at a piece of parchment lying before him on the stone next to a stick and a little bottle of ink.
On this parchment some notes had already been jotted down:
“The minutes are running, and I, Levi Matvei, am on Bald Mountain, and still there is no death!”
Further on:
“The sun is sinking, and there is no death.”
Now Levi Matvei hopelessly wrote with the sharpened stick:
“God! Why are you angry with him? Send him death.”
Having written this, he gave a tearless sob and again wounded his chest with his nails.

The cause of Levi’s despair lay in the terrible misfortune that had befallen Yeshua and himself, and, besides that, in the grave mistake which he, Levi, had in his own opinion made. The day before yesterday, in the daytime, Yeshua and Levi had been in Bethany near Yershalaim, where they were staying with a market gardener who had liked Yeshua’s preaching extremely. Both guests had worked all morning in the garden, helping their host, and toward evening they meant to walk to Yershalaim in the cool. But Yeshua for some reason grew hurried, said he had urgent business in the city, and left alone around noon. This was precisely where Levi Matvei’s first mistake lay. Why, why had he let him go alone!

In the evening Matvei was not able to go to Yershalaim. Some unexpected and terrible ailment struck him. He began to shake, his body filled with fire, his teeth began to chatter, and every minute he asked for something to drink. He could not go anywhere. He collapsed onto a horse blanket in the gardener’s shed and lay on it until the dawn of Friday, when the illness let go of Levi just as unexpectedly as it had attacked him. Though he was still weak and his legs trembled, he, tormented by some foreboding of disaster, took leave of his host and set off for Yershalaim. There he learned that his foreboding had not deceived him. Disaster had struck. Levi was in the crowd and heard the procurator announce the sentence.

When the condemned men were driven to the mountain, Levi Matvei ran alongside the line in the crowd of the curious, trying by some means to let Yeshua know, without being noticed, at least this much: that he, Levi, was here, with him, that he had not abandoned him on his last journey, and that he was praying for death to overtake Yeshua as quickly as possible. But Yeshua, looking into the distance, toward where he was being taken, did not, of course, see Levi.

And then, when the procession had gone about half a verst along the road, Matvei, who was being jostled in the crowd right by the line, was struck by a simple and brilliant thought, and at once, in his hot-headedness, he showered himself with curses for not having thought of it earlier. The soldiers were not marching in a tight line. There were gaps between them. With great agility and very precise calculation one could, bending low, slip between two legionaries, get through to the cart and leap onto it. Then Yeshua would be saved from torment.
One instant would be enough to stab Yeshua in the back with a knife, crying out to him: “Yeshua! I am saving you and going with you! I, Matvei, your faithful and only disciple!”

And if God blessed him with one more free instant, there might be time to stab himself too, escaping death on a post. However, this last point interested Levi, the former tax collector, very little. It made no difference to him how he perished. He wanted one thing: that Yeshua, who had never in his life done anyone the slightest harm, should escape torture.
The plan was very good, but the point was that Levi had no knife with him. Nor did he have a single coin of money.

Furious with himself, Levi got out of the crowd and ran back to the city. In his burning head leapt only one feverish thought: how, right now, by any means whatever, to get hold of a knife in the city and manage to catch up with the procession.

He ran as far as the city gate, weaving through the crush of caravans being sucked into the city, and saw on his left hand the open door of a little shop where bread was sold. Breathing heavily after running along the scorching road, Levi mastered himself, walked into the shop very sedately, greeted the woman who kept it, standing behind the counter, asked her to take down from the shelf the top loaf, which for some reason he liked better than the others, and, when she turned round, silently and quickly took from the counter the very thing that could not have been better—a long bread knife, sharpened like a razor—and at once dashed out of the shop.

A few minutes later he was again on the Jaffa road. But the procession could no longer be seen. He ran. At times he had to drop right down into the dust and lie motionless to get his breath back. And so he lay, astonishing the people riding on mules and walking on foot to Yershalaim. He lay listening to his heart pounding not only in his chest but in his head and in his ears. Having got his breath back a little, he would leap up and run on, but more and more slowly. When at last he caught sight of the long procession raising dust in the distance, it was already at the foot of the hill.
“O God...” Levi groaned, understanding that he was going to be late. And he was late.

When the fourth hour of the execution had run out, Levi’s torments reached their highest pitch, and he fell into a rage. Rising from the stone, he flung to the ground the knife, stolen in vain, as he now thought, crushed the flask with his foot, depriving himself of water, threw the keffiyeh off his head, seized his thin hair, and began to curse himself.
He cursed himself, shouting out senseless words, growled and spat, reviled his father and mother for bringing a fool into the world.

Seeing that his oaths and abuse had no effect and that nothing changed in the blazing sun because of them, he clenched his dry fists, shut his eyes tight, raised them to the sky, to the sun, which was creeping lower and lower, lengthening the shadows and going away to fall into the Mediterranean Sea, and demanded of God an immediate miracle. He demanded that God send Yeshua death at once.

Opening his eyes, he satisfied himself that on the hill everything was unchanged, except that the spots blazing on the centurion’s chest had gone out. The sun was sending its rays into the backs of the men being executed, who were turned with their faces toward Yershalaim. Then Levi shouted:
“I curse you, God!”
In a hoarse voice he shouted that he had become convinced of God’s injustice and did not intend to believe in him any longer.
“You are deaf!” Levi growled. “If you were not deaf, you would have heard me and killed him on the spot!”

Squeezing his eyes shut, Levi waited for the fire that would fall on him from the sky and strike him down. This did not happen, and, without unclenching his eyelids, Levi went on shouting caustic and insulting speeches at the sky. He shouted about his complete disillusionment and about there being other gods and religions. Yes, another god would not have allowed it, would never have allowed a man like Yeshua to be burned by the sun on a post.

“I was wrong!” shouted Levi, by now quite hoarse. “You are a god of evil! Or have your eyes been completely covered by the smoke from the censers of the temple, and have your ears ceased to hear anything but the trumpet blasts of the priests? You are not an almighty God. You are a black god. I curse you, god of robbers, their protector and their soul!”

At this something blew into the former tax collector’s face and something rustled under his feet. It blew again, and then, opening his eyes, Levi saw that everything in the world, whether under the influence of his curses or by virtue of some other causes, had changed. The sun had vanished before reaching the sea in which it drowned every evening. Having swallowed it, a storm cloud was rising across the sky from the west, menacingly and inexorably. Its edges were already boiling with white foam, its black smoky belly glinted yellow. The cloud was growling, and from time to time fiery threads fell out of it. Along the Jaffa road, along the meager Gihon valley, over the pilgrims’ tents, driven by the suddenly risen wind, columns of dust were flying.

Levi fell silent, trying to work out whether the storm that was about to cover Yershalaim would bring any change in the fate of the unfortunate Yeshua. And straight away, looking at the threads of fire slicing the cloud apart, he began to beg that the lightning might strike Yeshua’s post. Looking in repentance at the clear sky, which the cloud had not yet devoured and where the vultures were banking on the wing to get away from the storm, Levi thought that he had been insanely hasty with his curses: now God would not listen to him.

Turning his gaze to the foot of the hill, Levi fixed his eyes on the place where the cavalry regiment stood, spread out, and saw that significant changes had taken place there. From the height Levi managed to make out clearly how the soldiers were bustling about, pulling the lances out of the ground, how they were throwing their cloaks on, how the grooms were running toward the road at a jog, leading black horses by the bridle. The regiment was moving off, that was clear. Levi, shielding himself with his hand from the dust beating into his face and spitting, tried to work out what this could mean, that the cavalry was getting ready to leave? He shifted his gaze higher and made out a small figure in a crimson military chlamys climbing toward the place of execution. And at this the former tax collector’s heart went cold with the foreboding of a joyful end.

The man climbing the mountain in the fifth hour of the robbers’ sufferings was the commander of the cohort, who had galloped from Yershalaim accompanied by an orderly. At a wave from Ratslayer the line of soldiers opened, and the centurion saluted the tribune. The tribune, taking Ratslayer aside, whispered something to him. The centurion saluted a second time and moved toward the group of executioners who were sitting on stones at the foot of the posts. The tribune, for his part, directed his steps toward the one sitting on the three-legged stool, and the seated man politely rose to meet the tribune. The tribune said something to him too, in a low voice, and the two of them walked toward the posts. They were joined by the head of the temple guard as well.

Ratslayer, glancing with disgust at the dirty rags lying on the ground by the posts, rags that had recently been the criminals’ clothes, which the executioners had refused, called two of them over and ordered:
“Follow me!”

From the nearest post came a hoarse, senseless little song. Gestas, who hung on it, had gone mad from the flies and the sun by the end of the third hour of the execution and was now quietly singing something about grapes, but still, now and then, he shook his head, covered with a turban, and then the flies rose sluggishly from his face and came back onto it again.

Dismas, on the second post, suffered more than the other two, because oblivion did not overcome him, and he shook his head often and rhythmically, now to the right, now to the left, so as to strike his shoulder with his ear.

Yeshua was more fortunate than the other two. In the very first hour fainting fits began to strike him, and then he sank into oblivion, his head hanging in its unwound turban. The flies and horseflies had therefore covered him completely, so that his face disappeared under a black, stirring mask. In his groin, and on his belly, and under his arms sat fat horseflies, sucking at the yellow naked body.

Obeying the gestures of the man in the hood, one of the executioners took a spear, while another brought a bucket and a sponge to the post. The first executioner raised the spear and tapped with it first on one and then on the other of Yeshua’s arms, stretched out and tied with ropes to the crossbeam of the post. The body with its protruding ribs shuddered. The executioner drew the tip of the spear across the belly. Then Yeshua raised his head, and the flies lifted off with a buzz, and the face of the hanged man was revealed, swollen from bites, with puffed-up eyes, an unrecognizable face.
Unsticking his eyelids, Ha-Notsri looked down. His eyes, usually clear, were now somewhat clouded.
“Ha-Notsri!” said the executioner.
Ha-Notsri moved his swollen lips and responded in a hoarse robber’s voice:
“What do you want? Why have you come up to me?”

“Drink!” said the executioner, and the sponge soaked in water on the end of the spear rose to Yeshua’s lips. Joy flashed in his eyes; he pressed his mouth to the sponge and began greedily drinking in the moisture. From the neighboring post came the voice of Dismas:
“Injustice! I’m as much a robber as he is!”

Dismas strained, but could not move; his arms were held to the crossbeam in three places by loops of rope. He drew in his belly, dug his nails into the ends of the crossbeam, kept his head turned toward Yeshua’s post, and malice blazed in Dismas’s eyes.
A cloud of dust covered the place of execution, and it grew much darker. When the dust had blown away, the centurion shouted:
“Silence on the second post!”
Dismas fell silent. Yeshua tore himself away from the sponge and, trying to make his voice sound gentle and persuasive, and not succeeding, hoarsely asked the executioner:
“Give him a drink.”

It was growing darker and darker. The cloud had already flooded half the sky, pressing on toward Yershalaim; white boiling clouds raced ahead of the storm cloud, which was saturated with black moisture and fire. There was a flash and a crash right over the hill. The executioner took the sponge off the spear.
“Praise the magnanimous hegemon!” he whispered solemnly, and gently pierced Yeshua in the heart. Yeshua shuddered and whispered:
“Hegemon...”
Blood ran down his belly, his lower jaw twitched convulsively, and his head dropped.
At the second thunderclap the executioner was already giving Dismas a drink, and with the same words:
“Praise the hegemon!”—he killed him too.

Gestas, bereft of reason, gave a frightened cry as soon as the executioner was beside him, but when the sponge touched his lips, he growled something and sank his teeth into it. A few seconds later his body too sagged as far as the ropes allowed.

The man in the hood followed in the footsteps of the executioner and the centurion, and behind him came the head of the temple guard. Stopping at the first post, the man in the hood examined the bloodied Yeshua attentively, touched a foot with his white hand, and said to his companions:
“Dead.”
The same thing was repeated at the two other posts.

After this the tribune made a sign to the centurion and, turning, began to leave the top together with the head of the temple guard and the man in the hood. Half-darkness had fallen, and lightning furrowed the black sky. Suddenly fire spurted from it, and the centurion’s shout, “Break the cordon!” was drowned in the thunder. The happy soldiers rushed to run down the hill, putting on their helmets.
Darkness covered Yershalaim.

The downpour burst suddenly and caught the centuries halfway down the hill. The water came crashing down so terribly that, as the soldiers ran downhill, raging torrents were already flying after them. The soldiers slipped and fell in the sodden clay, hurrying to the level road along which—now barely visible through the curtain of water—the cavalry, soaked to the skin, was leaving for Yershalaim. A few minutes later, in the smoky brew of storm, water and fire, only one man remained on the hill.

Brandishing the knife he had not stolen in vain after all, slipping from the slippery ledges, clutching at whatever came to hand, sometimes crawling on his knees, he struggled toward the posts. Now he vanished in total murk, now he was suddenly lit up by a quivering light.

Reaching the posts, by now ankle-deep in water, he tore off his tallith, grown heavy and soaked through with water, was left in his shirt alone, and fell at Yeshua’s feet. He cut the ropes on his shins, climbed onto the lower crossbar, embraced Yeshua and freed his arms from the upper bonds. Yeshua’s naked, wet body collapsed onto Levi and knocked him to the ground. Levi wanted to heave it onto his shoulders at once, but some thought stopped him. He left on the ground, in the water, the body with its head thrown back and its arms flung wide, and ran, his feet sliding apart in the clay slush, to the other posts. He cut the ropes on them too, and two bodies collapsed onto the ground.
A few minutes passed, and on the top of the hill there remained only these two bodies and three empty posts. The water beat at these bodies and turned them over.
Neither Levi nor Yeshua’s body was on the top of the hill any longer by this time.
